current_episode.title: Episode 77: Featuring Julie Gondzar, Director of Development, Greater Portland Landmarks

guest.bio_context: Julie joined Greater Portland Landmarks in January 2025 after relocating from Wyoming, where she had lived and worked for several years. Originally from New England, she spent 18 years of her childhood in Scarborough and Portland, and holds a master's degree from Plymouth State University. She has extensive experience in both public and private sectors, with a background in science and prior work in water management and drought mitigation. She co-founded Snowy Elk Coffee Company with her husband in 2017, an award-winning specialty coffee roastery in Cheyenne, Wyoming, where she handled sales, marketing, and business development while building the brand and scaling operations before transitioning to her current role in nonprofit historic preservation.

context.transcript_excerpt: I'd like to welcome our listeners to the Bolas Beat Podcast. I'm your host, Greg Bolas. The Bolas Company is Northern New England's largest commercial real estate services firm with offices in Port and Maine, as well as Manchester and Portsmouth, New Hampshire. We've been selling and leasing real estate in Maine and New Hampshire since 1975. This podcast is designed to provide insight into Maine's leaders, its movers and shakers. And speaking of movers and shakers, I'd like to welcome Julie Gonza, Director of Development for Greater Portland Landmarks. Julie joined Greater Portland Landmarks as its Director of Development in January 2025, following her move from Wyoming. Originally from New England, she was excited to return and establish roots back in New England. Julie earned her master's degree from Plymouth State University and has extensive experience in both the public and private sectors. Her passion for historic preservation is deeply tied to Portland's history of marine culture, working ports, and beautiful architecture. Julie currently resides in Scarborough with her husband, Scott, and daughter, Abby. You'll find her enjoying the coast and the beaches year-round, whether surfing, paddleboarding, or fly fishing. She looks forward to connecting with supporters, engaging with the community, and championing preservation efforts. Welcome, Julie. Julie, you recently joined Greater Portland Landmarks after living and working in Wyoming. What drew you back to Maine and to this role specifically? I really was looking for more of a sense of community, and we really missed our family. So one of the main drivers for moving back to Maine was to be closer to family and have more of a sense of a community for myself, my husband, and our daughter. And I was also looking for a new career path. I have had a lot of different types of careers in my past, and I was really anxious to step into the nonprofit world. And my background has sort of led me naturally to the role of development. I love relationships. I love people. And I really wanted to support the preservation action that's been happening in southern Maine. And what I find interesting is you wear two different career hats. don't you? You're Director of Development at Great Important Landmarks, like we just talked about, but also founder and co-owner, I believe, of Snowy Elk Coffee Company based in Cheyenne, Wyoming. And with his background in food science and organic chemistry, we thought about opening a craft coffee roastery. The complexities of brewing beer are similar to the complexities of roasting coffee. It's based in Wyoming and it's really inspired by our love for outdoor adventure. We loved fly fishing out west, the hunting, the hiking, the camping. And so we were in the engine room for many, many years building this business, building the brand. I did a lot of the sales and marketing and business development. pending_qa.q: How can specialty beverage businesses leverage outdoor lifestyle branding to build national distribution?
pending_qa.r: Snowy Elk Coffee Company was inspired by a passion for outdoor adventure, including fly fishing, hunting, hiking, and camping. The brand was designed to represent that outdoor lifestyle. After spending years building the business and brand, the company hired key team members including an assistant roaster, fulfillment director, and CEO, which allowed them to train staff to run operations while scaling to ship coffee across the country.

pending_qa.q: What was the historical catalyst for the founding of Greater Portland Landmarks as an organization?
pending_qa.r: Greater Portland Landmarks was founded in 1964 following the 1961 demolition of Union Station on St. John Street. The passionate group of people who fought hard to save Union Station, which had been a huge transportation hub for Portland, ultimately became the organization. The iconic image of the clock tower coming down made people acutely aware of the importance of preservation.

pending_qa.q: How should preservation organizations balance advocacy with collaboration when engaging developers on historic buildings?
pending_qa.r: Greater Portland Landmarks has shifted from being confrontational to being proactive and collaborative. The organization now seeks to get a seat at the table early, be part of the planning process, and serve as a resource for developers. While the organization leans toward preservation, Julie emphasizes that success ultimately comes from collaboration rather than confrontational approaches, though advocacy groups must sometimes choose the right moments to push back hard.

pending_qa.q: What is the role and public access situation of the Portland Observatory on Munjoy Hill?
pending_qa.r: Greater Portland Landmarks is the steward of the Portland Observatory, which is owned by the City of Portland. The observatory is open May through October and facilitates tours to thousands of visitors every year from all over the world. The building originally served as a signal tower where flags would be raised to alert the community about incoming ships, and educational displays explain its history and the reconstructions that have been done over the years.

pending_qa.q: How does historic preservation contribute to a city's economic development and quality of life?
pending_qa.r: Preservation brings in people, keeps the economy strong, and attracts businesses and residents. People want to visit and live in Portland because of its character and historic architecture. Preservation ultimately increases quality of life, and if a city loses its unique, distinctive character, it will lose people. The working waterfront and historic districts drive tourism and business activity, making for a good market and strong economy.

pending_qa.q: What misconceptions do developers hold about the barriers to historic preservation projects?
pending_qa.r: One of the biggest misconceptions is that there are heavy barriers that cannot be passed. Julie states that preservation should not be as scary as perceived, and there are lots of solutions and opportunity to be creative. While there may be some limitations, in many cases if people understand the value of preservation, they can change, alter, and improve properties while preserving important elements.

pending_qa.q: What are examples of successful adaptive reuse projects that balance historic preservation with modern development in Portland?
pending_qa.r: The Monument Hotel, developed by Jim Brady, is restoring a former bank building using historic tax credits and combining preserved elements like marble walls and original structures with modern updates. The Safford House at 93 High Street, now owned by Woodhull, was preserved and modernized into office space, winning a preservation award while maintaining the feeling of an old building with preserved cabinets and woodworking.

pending_qa.q: What is the current status and preservation strategy for the U.S. Custom House in Portland?
pending_qa.r: The U.S. Custom House faces a possibility that the federal government will dispose of the building. Greater Portland Landmarks is being proactive by working with the city and a group called Friends of the U.S. Custom House to develop a feasibility study and plan for future use, so the organization will be ready with a preservation strategy if the building transitions out of federal ownership. The building is currently not open to the public and contains incredible historic architecture.
